title: The Council of Jerusalem
lead: The meeting of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, around AD 48–49, that decided Gentile believers did not have to be circumcised or keep the whole law of Moses, but should keep away from food sacrificed to idols, blood, strangled meat and sexual sin (Acts 15). Paul's own account of a Jerusalem meeting (Galatians 2:1–10) may describe the same event. Churches have looked to it ever since as the first church council.

sections.b: Israel's Scriptures promised that the nations would one day turn to the God of Israel (Isaiah 2:2–4; Zechariah 8:20–23), and the Torah had laws both for converts, who were circumcised (Exodus 12:48), and for resident foreigners, who were not (Leviticus 17–18). When Gentiles began to believe in Jesus as Israel's Messiah, first Cornelius (Acts 10–11) and then many in Antioch and the cities of the first journey (Acts 11:20–26; 13–14), the church had to decide which model applied. Some Jewish believers held that Gentiles must be circumcised to be saved (Acts 15:1, 5). The council decided they need not.
sections.refs: Genesis 17:9–14; Exodus 12:48; Leviticus 17:8–15; Isaiah 2:2–4; Zechariah 8:20–23; Acts 10:1–48; Acts 15:1–29

sections.b: Acts has Paul deliver the decree to the churches (Acts 16:4) and James remind him of it years later (Acts 21:25). Paul's letters never cite it: he deals with idol food on his own terms (1 Corinthians 8–10; Romans 14), and in Galatians he reports only that the Jerusalem leaders added nothing to his gospel except care for the poor (Galatians 2:6–10). Yet the incident at Antioch, where Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles (Galatians 2:11–14), shows the issue of shared meals was not settled at once. Revelation still condemns eating food sacrificed to idols (Revelation 2:14, 20), and many churches of the second and third centuries kept the ban on blood.
sections.refs: Acts 16:4; Acts 21:25; Galatians 2:1–14; 1 Corinthians 8:1–13; 1 Corinthians 10:14–33; Romans 14:1–23; Revelation 2:14; Revelation 2:20
